conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Lee, a perinatal mental-health clinician. Over the next few minutes we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS, to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. It’s simply a 10-question conversation that helps us spot any signs of depression or anxiety that can creep up in the first year postpartum. Everything you share stays between us unless there’s an immediate safety concern, so please answer as openly as you feel comfortable. Ready to start?  

First, thinking about the past seven days: have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Honestly… I still laugh, but it’s not as easy or natural as it used to be. Sometimes my partner will joke around and I’ll force a smile more than actually feel amused—like the joy is muffled. It’s not impossible, just… harder.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I can still laugh sometimes, but it feels like I have to work for it—like I’m not getting the same lift from funny moments that I used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some things—like taking the baby for a short walk or having my morning coffee—but the excitement feels kind of muted. It’s more "that’ll be nice" than the real buzz I used to get.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. If the baby’s fussy and I can’t settle him right away, I’ll think, “I must be missing something,” or “Other moms would have this figured out.” It’s not constant, but little things make me wonder if I’m falling short somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason
I do feel anxious, mostly about the baby—like is he breathing okay when he’s napping or am I doing the feedings right. It’s not all day, but it pops up even when nothing’s actually wrong.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes I’ll get this sudden tight-chest feeling out of nowhere—like a little wave of panic—especially when the baby’s asleep and the house is too quiet. It passes pretty quickly, but it’s unsettling because I can’t point to any real danger.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes. There are stretches—especially in the late afternoon when I’m running on almost no sleep—where every tiny thing feels like one more log on an already heavy pile. I’ll think, “How am I going to keep this up?” and feel sort of swallowed by the to-do list.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m that unhappy, but I do have trouble sleeping a few nights a week. My mind just keeps ticking through baby stuff—did I sterilize the bottles, is his rash getting worse—and then I’m wide awake even when he’s settled.
I have felt sad or miserable
I do get sad sometimes—like this heavy feeling just settles in. It’s not all day, but when it hits, everything feels a little gray, even the happy baby moments.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I haven’t cried much at all—maybe once or twice in the past week when I got really overwhelmed. Mostly I just feel kind of flat rather than tearful.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I might feel tired or down, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 16: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: ___________  Weeks Postpartum: ___

A. Patient-Reported Symptoms (endorsed items)  
- Diminished ability to experience pleasure/humor (Q1, Q2)  
- Episodic low mood, “flat” affect, mild anhedonia (Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt over routine infant care (Q3)  
- Recurrent intrusive worry about infant safety; occasional panic-like surges (Q4, Q5)  
- Frequent feeling overwhelmed, especially late afternoon/evening (Q6)  
- Sleep-onset difficulty linked to ruminating about infant needs (Q7)  
- Rare tearfulness (1–2 episodes/week) when fatigued (Q9)

B. Pattern Summary  
Mild-to-moderate depressive and anxiety symptoms, situational rather than pervasive; no suicidal ideation (Q10 denied). Function is preserved but strained by fatigue and worry.

C. Screening Risk Indicators  
✓ Low mood / anhedonia  
✓ Guilt / self-criticism  
✓ Sleep disturbance with mood component  
✓ Anxiety/panic without clear precipitant  
✗ No self-harm ideation (safety concern: absent)

D. Clinical Impression (screening level only)  
Findings are above baseline baby-blues threshold; meet partial criteria for minor depression and comorbid postpartum anxiety. Recommend formal diagnostic interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS) and psychoeducation on coping, rest, support systems.

E. Safety  
No suicidal/homicidal ideation expressed; no protective concerns identified at this time.

F. Next Steps  
- Complete validated EPDS; review score with provider  
- Discuss sleep hygiene, respite care, peer support resources  
- Follow-up visit within 1–2 weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen
